name: hey
what_it_is: hey is a lightweight CLI HTTP load generator and ApacheBench (ab) replacement, written in Go. It sends a configurable number of concurrent requests to a target URL and prints latency/throughput statistics.
components: hey (single Go binary — both the CLI entry point and the load engine)
requester package (internal library handling request dispatch, timing, and result collection)
measurement: Total requests sent and success/failure counts
Response latency distribution (mean, min, max, percentiles)
DNS lookup, connection, and TTFB timing breakdown
CSV output mode for raw per-request metrics (-o csv)
configuration: -m: HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS)
-d: request body string; -D: request body from file
-cpus: number of CPU cores to use
-o: output format (default summary; csv for raw data)
fault_injection: No built-in fault injection — hey is a client-side load generator only
Redirect following can be disabled (-disable-redirects) to observe redirect responses
Keep-alive can be disabled (-disable-keepalive) to force fresh TCP connections per request
modes: Fixed-count mode: run exactly N requests (-n), default 200
Duration mode: run for a fixed wall-clock duration (-z), e.g. -z 30s or -z 3m
Rate-limited mode: cap QPS per worker (-q)
CSV reporting mode: emit per-request metrics as CSV (-o csv)
constraints: Total requests (-n) must not be smaller than the concurrency level (-c); hey will error if n < c
hey is a pure HTTP client — it cannot load-test non-HTTP protocols (TCP, gRPC, WebSocket)
No built-in result persistence; output goes to stdout only (redirect to file for storage)
No distributed/multi-node mode; all load originates from a single process on one machine
Docker image is built FROM scratch with no shell — cannot be exec'd into or used interactively beyond the entrypoint
docker_services: hey (single-stage scratch image; entrypoint /hey; no exposed ports, no volumes defined in Dockerfile)
notable_absences: No docker-compose.yml — hey has no server-side component requiring orchestration
No warm-up phase or ramp-up concurrency control
No built-in think time / sleep between requests
No scenario scripting or request sequencing
No WebSocket, gRPC, or raw TCP support
No HTML/JSON dashboard or real-time progress display (only final summary)
